24447: Chronicles was written after the exile, when Jewish thought increasingly attributed evil to an adversary figure rather than directly to God. The Chronicler reworked his source to avoid saying God incited sin. The Hebrew in 1 Chr 21:1 has 'satan' without the article, which may be a proper name or simply 'an adversary'.
24450: Since *satan* can mean any adversary (it is used of human opponents), 1 Chr 21:1 might refer to a hostile foreign power or official whose threat provoked the census. This is possible but less widely held.
24451: One book says God did it, the other says Satan. That is a direct contradiction, and the number differences prove the texts are unreliable.
24452: On the inciter: harmonisers point to the Bible's repeated pattern of God working through evil agents (Job, 1 Kings 22), so both statements can be true at different levels. Critical scholars see a deliberate theological revision by the Chronicler, which is a change of emphasis rather than careless error. On the numbers: harmonisers suggest different counting bases (e.g. including or excluding certain groups) and scribal copying errors, which are common with numerals; critics see the Chronicler's own adjustments. Readers should know both explanations; neither side disputes that the Chronicler worked from Samuel.
24453: When bad things happen, the Bible neither makes God the author of evil in a simple way nor removes him from the picture. Hold God's sovereignty and human responsibility together, as David did when he confessed his own sin.
24455: Matthew says Judas threw the silver into the temple and went and hanged himself; the priests then bought a potter's field with the money. Acts says Judas acquired a field with the reward and, falling headlong, burst open. Both call the place the Field of Blood.
24456: Both accounts agree Judas died shamefully and that a field called Akeldama was linked to the money; they differ on details and on why it got its name.
24458: Judas returned the money, hanged himself; the priests bought the potter's field, called the Field of Blood because blood money bought it.
24460: Judas acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness; falling headlong he burst open, and it was called Akeldama, Field of Blood.
24461: Did Judas hang himself or fall? Did he buy the field or did the priests? Why was it called the Field of Blood: because of blood money or because of his blood?
24463: Traditional harmonisation, widely held in conservative commentary
24464: Judas hanged himself; later the rope or branch gave way (or the body was cut down after decomposing) and it fell and burst. The priests bought the field with Judas's money, so it could be said he 'acquired' it through them. Both reasons for the name could be true.
24467: The Greek *prenes genomenos*, usually 'falling headlong', may mean 'swelling up', which would fit a decomposing body and an early tradition (Papias, preserved by later writers) that Judas swelled grotesquely. This is debated.
24470: Each writer shapes the story to fulfil Scripture. Matthew draws on Zechariah's thirty pieces thrown to the potter and Jeremiah's field purchase, and his hanging echoes Ahithophel, David's betrayer. Luke links the death to psalms about the wicked's dwelling being desolate. The theological framing explains the different emphases.
24473: Early Christians knew Judas died badly and that a Jerusalem plot called Akeldama was linked with him, but separate traditions explained it differently. The accounts cannot be fully harmonised, and that is evidence the writers did not copy one another.
24474: Matthew and Acts contradict each other on Judas's death, who bought the field and why it was named. Matthew even attributes a Zechariah prophecy to Jeremiah.
24475: Harmonisers offer a plausible sequence (hanging then falling) and note that a purchase made with someone's money can be described as theirs. Literary readers note that each author frames the death through different Scriptures; Matthew's 'Jeremiah' may reflect a combined quotation, since the potter and a field purchase both appear in Jeremiah (Jer 18:1-4, Jer 32:6-9). Critical scholars accept that the accounts preserve different traditions. All agree on the core: Judas died soon, in disgrace, and the money was tied to a field known as the Field of Blood.
24476: Judas's end is a warning about despair as well as betrayal. Contrast Peter, who also failed Jesus but returned and was restored (John 21:15-17).
